prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The case is that this is a complete chain from hormone physiology (proglucagon processing, the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, secretion and receptor biology, gut-pancreas-brain signalling) to therapies with large randomized outcome evidence in type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiorenal disease. The principle has been independently confirmed for years, the interpretation is stable, and the clinical consequence is exceptional. I keep a basic-discovery trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov because the Nobel prize in this category has traditionally rewarded the discovery of a physiological mechanism, with therapeutic consequence as the proof of its importance.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The three-person limit forces an exclusion that is hard to defend: either Knudsen, whose long-acting acylated analogues made the drugs actually work, or Mojsov, whose identification of the active peptide is contested by the Habener group (not on our list). A basic trio can look as if it ignores the people who produced the medicines, and a trio with Knudsen can look as if it underweights who defined the biology. Priority disputes and patent history are also not something I can settle from the supplied record.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen as a coherent arc across physiology and drug development, and treats Mojsov as a real but not fully accommodable credit question.
responses.response: I take this seriously and it is the closest rival to my own trio. I still differ: Knudsen's work is decisive for the drugs, but the prize question is who discovered the physiological principle, and the active-peptide identification is on the discovery side. Replacing Mojsov by Knudsen turns the prize into a drug-development award, and I would want that argued explicitly rather than reached by default. I concede the point is not clear cut, and I would reconsider if the committee judges the Mojsov priority claim too contested to cite with confidence.

responses.point: Sandberg backs Drucker, Holst and Mojsov and argues that Knudsen's industry-development role may be better recognised separately or not at all; he also ranks massively parallel sequencing (B003) second.
responses.response: I agree on the GLP-1 configuration. On B003 I disagree with ranking it second: sequencing is an enabling technology whose impact is exceptional, but the shortlist shows only one member ranking it and the Mayer versus Cambridge question is unresolved. In my own ranking it is not in the top group, and I do not think opening support from one colleague justifies putting it ahead of CAR-T or optogenetics. I would be persuaded if Rickard shows that the case for technology prizes in this category is stronger than I give it credit for.

responses.point: Perlmann gives GLP-1 first and ranks CAR-T second with a two-person June and Sadelain pair, regarding Rosenberg as a distinct adoptive-therapy lineage; he also places UPR (B043) third.
responses.response: I agree that Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is a different lineage from the engineered chimeric receptor, and my own opening ranking of CAR-T fourth reflected that I could not make the three-person credit clean. I do not share the third place for the unfolded protein response: the mechanism is clear and Walter and Mori are a clean pair, but the clinical consequence is largely prospective, which I weigh less than an established therapeutic principle such as CAR-T. This is a difference of weighting rather than of fact.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, ranks optogenetics third and asks whether a tool or method fits the prize as well as a disease-oriented discovery, while acknowledging that Boyden, Bamberg and Miesenboeck have strong claims.
responses.response: This is the question I find hardest, partly because the field is close to mine, so I have tried to evaluate it on the record. Channelrhodopsin discovery and its transfer to neurons changed how circuits are dissected, but six credited people cannot fit into three places and any selection will be disputed, with a prize history of method awards offering no clean guide. For that reason I keep it as an alternative rather than my preferred configuration; the clinical translation (vision restoration) is still early.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks cGAS-STING second, emphasising its direct relevance to interferonopathies and lupus, with Chen and Barber as the two core names.
responses.response: The mechanism is convincing and the Chen and Barber pairing is the most defensible within five names, but I would not place it second. The clinical benefit of STING modulation is not yet demonstrated, so it is a discovery prize on mechanism alone, whereas GLP-1 and CAR-T already have outcome evidence. I would put it ahead of optogenetics only if the committee decides mechanism without therapy is enough, and the allocation between Barber and Ishikawa remains open.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should take the third place, and how to weigh the contested early peptide identification (Habener group not on the list).
Whether the committee wants to frame the prize around physiology or around the engineered drugs, which determines the citation and the laureate set.
For the alternatives, how to cut six optogenetics names to three, and whether the supplied CAR-T credit omits the originator of the chimeric receptor concept.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates: none of the credited names for B016, B007, B008 or the other shortlisted ballots is a documented collaborator, mentor or institutional colleague. My neuroscience field overlaps with optogenetics (B008) as a user community, which I note for transparency; my documented ties are to Grillner, Ernfors and Perlmann (a committee colleague, 2009 paper), none of whom is a candidate here.
